entry.summary: In July I wrote a 56-line shell script called mcp-optional whose entire job was to remove two MCP servers from my config. Not fix them. Remove them. Both were stdio servers, so each one spawns its own Node process per session. entry.summary: The tool built over the last four posts asks the catalog the same questions again and again. summary alone is six requests, one per magnitude band plus one for the strongest event. Run it, change the end date by a day, run it again, and five of those six answers were already on your screen a moment ago. So the client wants a cache. The awkward part is not writing one. entry.title: Typing is the fastest way to actually learn kana — most learners skip it
entry.summary:
Typing is the fastest way to actually learn kana — most learners skip it
If you're learning Japanese, you've probably spent an afternoon staring at a hiragana chart. あ, い, う, え, お — fine. か, き, く, け, こ — got it. By the end of the hour you can recognize all 46 characters when you see them in order. Then you open a real Japanese sentence and freeze. You recognize the shapes, but your brain still needs two seconds per character to convert け to "ke". Recognition and recall are different skills. Charts train the first. Typing trains the second — and it's the one that actually makes you fluent. Kana charts are great for introduction. They're terrible for retention. Here's why: You read them in a fixed order (あいうえお), so you memorize the sequence, not the characters. You get no output practice —…
